title: Interphase chromosome conformation is specified by distinct folding programmes inherited through mitotic chromosomes or the cytoplasm

authors.name: Allana Schooley

abstract: Identity-specific chromosome conformation must be re-established at each cell division. To uncover how interphase folding is inherited, we developed an approach that segregates chromosome-intrinsic mechanisms from those propagated through the cytoplasm during G1 nuclear reassembly. Inducible degradation of proteins essential for the establishment of nucleocytoplasmic transport during mitotic exit enabled analysis of folding programmes with distinct modes of inheritance. Here we show that genome compartmentalization is driven entirely by chromosome-intrinsic factors. In addition to conventional compartmental segregation, the chromosome-intrinsic folding programme leads to prominent genome-scale microcompartmentalization of mitotically bookmarked cis-regulatory elements. The microcompartment conformation forms transiently during telophase and is subsequently modulated by a second folding programme inherited through the cytoplasm in early G1. This programme includes cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and factors involved in transcription and RNA processing. The combined and interdependent action of chromosome-intrinsic and cytoplasmic inherited folding programmes determines the interphase chromatin conformation as cells exit mitosis.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This Nature Cell Biology article has already shown measurable scholarly traction, with 13 citations, 14 documented downstream reuses, and a field- and year-normalized position in the top 10% of cited work. Its strongest impact signal is conceptual: it addresses a fundamental question in chromosome biology by distinguishing folding programs inherited through mitotic chromosomes from those carried by the cytoplasm during G1 nuclear reassembly.

Full narrative

The study advances a central problem in cell biology: how interphase chromosome organization is re-established after cell division. By separating chromosome-intrinsic mechanisms from cytoplasmic influences during nuclear reassembly, the authors offer an experimental framework for tracing how distinct folding programs are inherited. That framing appears to have resonated quickly within the chromatin and genome-organization communities, consistent with the paper’s top-10%-citation standing for its field and year.

The citation record shows early but meaningful uptake across a focused disciplinary landscape. Citing work appears in venues such as Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, Nature Protocols, Nature Genetics, Molecular Cell, Nature Communications, and related preprints, indicating that the article is being used by researchers working on 3D genome organization, mitosis, nuclear structure, and chromatin regulation. The reuse graph likewise suggests broader methodological and conceptual influence, with downstream works spanning articles, preprints, and a biomedical article mention in Europe PMC.

The surrounding record also points to a well-supported research program. The article is associated with multiple funders, including NIH/NHGRI support and Howard Hughes Medical Institute backing, and it is linked to openly available research infrastructure through GitHub and Zenodo records. Those stewardship signals matter because they make it easier for other groups to inspect, adapt, and build on the work, which helps explain the early downstream reuse already visible.

Public discourse in the usual event-data sources is not available here, so the impact story is currently strongest in scholarly channels rather than in broad public attention. Even so, the combination of selective citations, high-impact citing venues, and documented reuse suggests that this article has begun to shape how researchers think about chromosome folding inheritance at mitotic exit, especially in studies connecting chromatin dynamics with nuclear reassembly and cell-cycle progression.
